transcript.text: Architects in New Zealand in the early 20th century were big fans of traditional styles.
At that time, they often looked to European models for inspiration
and perceived building design from a traditional perspective.
The climate, for example, was the top concern when designing the roof.
Weather conditions across the country can vary significantly
and regions with frequent rain needed special attention.
In areas where the annual precipitation is high, ensuring water could drain efficiently
was essential for protecting the structure and longevity of the building.
Therefore, proper drainage systems had to be considered.
Wood was the most popular choice for house building, mainly due to its availability,
cost effectiveness and ease of use.
Other materials either weren't affordable or simply weren't accessible
in rural parts of the country at the time.
The majority of traditional buildings are square in shape and this wasn't by accident.
It was a strategic choice.
Straight lines and right angles are easier to construct and more space efficient.
Architects believed this approach helped to maximize utilization of interior space,
especially in areas where plots of land were relatively small.
Additionally, avoiding unusual shapes like curves and diagonal corners
made furnishing the interiors much more straightforward.
Complex forms not only wasted valuable room but also posed problems
when arranging furniture or installing fixtures.
As the country progressed, there were several changes New Zealand architects embraced in the 1960s.
These changes reflected not only a shift in design philosophy but also improvements in technology
and construction methods.
The first was a shift to concrete as a material which gradually replaced timber
in many modern buildings.
This transition was made possible by construction techniques introduced by immigrants
from Europe and Japan who brought with them advanced machinery and engineering knowledge.
At the same time, New Zealand, like many other nations, was dealing with financial constraints
following global events.
Because of the economic impact of the Second World War, resources had to be used wisely.
As a result, both private developers and government-backed construction projects
were focused on the cost of construction.
Minimizing expense while maximizing utility became the dominant goal during this period.
That's one of the key factors they considered.
They pursued economical designs.
Somiles Warren's architecture offers a classic example of this country's architectural styles at that time.
He became well known for modernizing the traditional aesthetic and for using geometric forms in innovative ways.
In many of his works, he integrated repetitive block-like shapes into his works, a feature that became a hallmark of his style.
This approach came to be associated with a trend in architecture called brutalism,
which emphasized raw materials and strong bold structures.
At the same time, the use of natural materials was changing.
He, like others, abandoned some expensive materials such as stone, not just for economic reasons, but also for practicality and mass construction.
Meanwhile, car ownership was on the rise, and families were becoming increasingly reliant on private vehicles for commuting and daily tasks.
As a result, equipping each new house with a garage gradually became trendy.
This change was seen not just as a convenience, but as a necessity that architects needed to incorporate into every design for suburban homes.
Among other modern housing styles, Lockwood Homes, which featured identical walls, stood out for their uniformity and efficient production.
These homes were mass-produced and became popular for their quick assembly and affordability.
They also gained in popularity, especially among working-class families.
However, the design was not without its critics.
Some architects and homeowners felt it lacked variety and personal expression, and the buildings were also criticised for this characteristic.
A sameness that didn't allow much room for individuality or creativity in layout.
Still, few people would have doubts about the architectural changes of this era, especially considering how widespread and influential they became.
In urban centres, industrial or business complexes have been designed to resemble towers, a departure from earlier, more horizontal layouts.
These tall structures helped maximise space in crowded city districts and symbolised economic development.
This has happened elsewhere in some industrialised countries, following similar trends seen in places like the UK and Japan.
In addition to the overall shape, which served a functional purpose, architects also concentrated on the visual appeal of some tall designs, such as shadow and colours.
These finer aesthetic elements helped modern buildings feel less sterile and more engaging to the eye, improving both their beauty and their emotional impact on residents and visitors alike.
